name: Sam Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a bricklaying gang on building sites, setting corners, checking the lines and making sure the scaffold is ready before the young ones climb it. I earned a trade certificate, but most of what I know came from walls that showed me my mistakes. I sometimes ask an AI tool to tidy a materials note, then count the bricks myself. My partner and I have grown children; work pays less than it should, we have under a month of expenses saved, and there are few other crews hiring nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang a tidy materials note is useful, but it will not lay a straight wall. I already use AI occasionally for the wording and still count every pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect a small office change to take my trowel away. The thin reserve is the real problem: if the next site starts late, our household will be short before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking bricklaying shifts and checking deliveries at the gate. In the first year I would put part of any paid Saturday work into savings, if the contractor offers it, and keep using AI only to tidy messages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a gap between contracts, though this picture itself is mild. My partner can tell when I start counting Saturdays before they are offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What amount could you save from Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One quarter of each paid Saturday would go aside, after the utility and grocery bills are covered. I will not pretend a weekend shift is money until it is worked and paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the next site is delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor for a confirmed start date and take any ordinary bricklaying shifts still on offer. There are not many other crews within a reasonable drive.

say: **Office AI** can tidy a note without laying a straight brick wall.
I still **count pallets** before the gang starts.
think: A delayed **site start** could leave our household short.
Our **thin reserve** matters more now than a small software change.
do: **Keep** leading bricklaying shifts and checking materials deliveries at the site gate.
**Save** one quarter of paid Saturday earnings when available.
S0.quote: I will not pretend a weekend shift is money until it is worked and paid.
fieldNote: His **existing AI use** is occasional message drafting, followed by his own material count.
New **Saturday saving** depends on actual paid work; the household cannot rely on unoffered shifts.

steps.text: Keep bricklaying shifts and check pallet deliveries
Save one quarter of paid Saturday earnings when available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say an office system might order bricks and schedule deliveries faster, but the crew must keep the final check. If software shortens our building time, the contractor should show how the wall stays safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster schedule could cut my paid hours if the gang cannot meet it, and I cannot simply move to another local builder. I am willing to learn a proven site scheduling tool, but only with paid training time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare one new digital delivery plan with our last three jobs and mark where the loads arrived late. In the first year I would take the contractor’s AI scheduling class if there is an actual funded place on paid time, then keep working the wall while I test its estimates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a timetable turning into fewer shifts. I would rather learn what the screen means than let someone far from the scaffold decide our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery time against when the scaffold was ready and when the mortar was mixed. A pallet on paper is no use if a truck blocks the wrong gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if training is offered after hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid hours or stay with my current way of checking plans. Our household cannot afford an unpaid evening course for the contractor’s tool.

say: **Delivery software** may help if the gang keeps its final safety check.
Shorter **building times** need evidence from the actual site.
think: A digital **schedule** could cut paid hours.
Few **nearby builders** make a job switch hard if hours fall.
do: **Compare** a digital delivery plan with three previous building jobs.
**Take** a funded AI scheduling class if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Keep** checking wall work against the new estimates.
S1.quote: A pallet on paper is no use if a truck blocks the wrong gate.
fieldNote: He will **test AI** against concrete site records before trusting it.
His **learning plan** requires an actual funded class place during regular paid work hours.

steps.text: Take funded AI scheduling class if actual paid-time place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger bricklayers that AGI may run buying and planning by 2028, but people-level robots on site follow around 2031. An apprentice still needs to learn how a wall carries weight during those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on part may buy me time, but a bricklaying robot could take the final wages my partner and I need. I cannot treat retirement as an escape while our savings cover less than one month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the contractor about an actual funded, paid-time robot masonry safety course and keep teaching the apprentice line and level. If a course place opens, I would take it; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local site-inspection job only if its hours and wage cover our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing work near the end of my earning years. A machine can lay bricks in a demonstration; I want to see who checks the wall after rain and movement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the course to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking bonds, levels and scaffold clearances on a machine-built wall, with a person allowed to stop unsafe work. I would not pay for a course that is only a sales film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no inspection vacancy appears locally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the bricklaying shifts while they exist and ask which actual builders are hiring. I cannot move my partner on the promise of a job.

say: **2028 AGI** reaches buying before capable bricklaying robots around 2031.
Apprentices must learn **wall safety** during the hand-work years.
think: A **site robot** could remove wages I still need.
Under **one month saved** makes retirement unaffordable without real figures.
do: **Seek** a funded paid-time robot masonry safety course.
**Attend** if an actual place opens and continue teaching the apprentice.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only at bill-covering hours and pay.
S2.quote: A machine can lay bricks in a demonstration; I want to see who checks the wall after rain and movement.
fieldNote: His **course condition** requires an actual place, funding, paid time and site safety content.
He would **apply locally** only to a posted inspection role with enough hours and wages.

steps.text: Keep bricklaying shifts and teach apprentice wall checks
Take funded robot masonry safety course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection job if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang five years is enough to try a robot on a test wall before allowing one on occupied building work. The date for capable site robots is about 2034, so safety checks should be settled before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to work until that point, but that depends on site contracts and my health. I could consider stopping earlier than I had hoped if our household income and bills allow it, though today’s savings do not give us that option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep supervising the gang and review our household income and retirement costs with my partner each year. In the first year after 2031 I would take a funded paid-time robot inspection course if a real place runs, then apply for a posted local inspection role only if its wage and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, but five years gives me time to judge a real trial. I would not stake the family budget on a machine maker’s promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a test wall have to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs to stay true under load and weather, and a bricklayer must be able to inspect the bond and stop the robot. I would watch a whole job, not a single perfect row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop site work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after my partner and I compare dependable income against housing, food and healthcare costs. If the money is short, I would need paid work even after the robots arrive.

say: **2031 AGI** allows time for a real robot masonry trial before around 2034.
A bricklayer needs **stop authority** on a machine-built wall.
think: Retirement before **2034** is possible only if household income covers costs.
Thin **savings** and uncertain contracts make that unlikely today.
do: **Keep** supervising bricklaying and review retirement costs yearly.
**Take** funded robot inspection training if an actual paid-time place runs.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only with bill-covering pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to watch a proper trial.
S3.quote: I would not stake the family budget on a machine maker’s promise.
fieldNote: He considers **retirement before robots** only if actual household income covers retirement costs.
He keeps **training and job moves** tied to real funded places and bill-covering local vacancies.

steps.text: Keep supervising masonry and review retirement affordability yearly
Take funded robot inspection course if actual paid-time place runs
Apply after funded course for posted local inspection job if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children a decade before AGI is useful if building work still pays through it. Office planning might change in 2036; capable bricklaying robots would follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had imagined eventually handing the trowel to an apprentice and cutting my days, but our savings do not support that yet. If site work dries up after 2036, I would need a real alternative, even if the robot itself is still three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the gang and put part of any paid extra shifts into savings now. Each autumn I would check retirement costs with my partner; if after 2036 our bricklaying hours fall, I would take a funded paid-time inspection course only with an actual place, then apply for a posted local inspection vacancy only if its pay and hours cover bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about whether paid building jobs will last long enough. Ten years gives us a chance to save, but it is not ten years of guaranteed pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your first sign that hours are falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contractor stops booking the next site before we finish the present wall. I would ask for a written schedule, then start checking actual local vacancy notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family help replace a wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children would lend a hand in an emergency, but they have their own homes to run. I would rather earn and save from paid shifts than plan around their money.

say: **2036 AGI** changes plans before capable bricklaying robots around 2039.
A decade helps only if **building wages** keep arriving.
think: I want fewer **trowel days** eventually, but current savings cannot pay for them.
Falling **site hours** after 2036 would force another work plan.
do: **Keep** leading the gang and save part of paid extra shifts.
**Review** retirement costs each autumn with my partner.
**Train** and apply if hours fall, with a funded place and bill-covering local posting.
feel: **Anxious** about the continuity of paid site work.
S4.quote: Ten years gives us a chance to save, but it is not ten years of guaranteed pay.
fieldNote: His **extra saving** comes only from new paid shifts, not existing cash.
Post-2036 **training and applications** need falling hours, an actual paid course place and a posted local job with sufficient pay.

steps.text: Keep leading bricklaying gang and review retirement costs annually

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robot date is close and there is hardly a month of money behind us. Paid, funded masonry safety training with an actual place and a posted local inspection job at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I hope the younger bricklayers keep learning from a real wall. An apprenticeship should teach young bricklayers what to do when a drawing and a brick disagree.

portrait: **Sam Varga**, 58, leads a bricklaying crew on building sites and has a vocational trade certificate.
He and his **partner** have grown children, lower pay, under one month saved and few similar jobs nearby.
He uses **AI occasionally** for materials messages but verifies quantities and waits for proof before adopting new scheduling tools.
He is **anxious** about paid hours across scenarios, and prefers apprenticeships and work over depending on family money.
He seeks **funded paid training** and local inspection work only when actual openings and household bills support the move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only about three years before capable robots could threaten his needed bricklaying wages.
whatWouldHelp: A real **funded course place** on paid time and a posted local inspection role at bill-covering pay would help.
headlineQuote: An apprenticeship should teach young bricklayers what to do when a drawing and a brick disagree.
